extracted.intended_audience: recipients of federal education funds (K-12 and postsecondary institutions), school administrators, HR departments, and legal counsel responsible for Title IX compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretation and implementation guidance for Title IX provisions addressing pregnancy and pregnancy-related conditions for students and employees, including comparability, reasonable modifications, certification requirements, and employment protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.40(b)(4) comparability of pregnancy-related conditions to other temporary medical conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.40(b)(4) states that, to the extent consistent with paragraph (b)(3), a recipient must treat pregnancy or related conditions in the same manner and under the same policies as any other temporary medical condition with respect to any medical or hospital benefit, service, plan, or policy the recipient administers, operates, offers, or participates in with respect to students admitted to the recipient's education program or activity. The Department removed references to “disability” and changed “physical condition” to “medical condition.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies only when doing so would not deny or limit any person's rights or the recipient's obligations under §106.40(b)(3). Examples: if a recipient's medical/disability policy provides more generous breaks or services for non-pregnancy temporary conditions, those more generous policies must be applied to pregnant students; if the non-pregnancy policy is less generous than required reasonable modifications for a pregnant student, the less generous policy cannot be applied to the pregnant student. The provision also prohibits recipient policies that treat pregnant students differently (e.g., excluding pregnant students from tutoring that is available to others), even if no individual requests a modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.40(b)(3) reasonable modifications floor for students
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.40(b)(3) requires recipients to take specific actions to prevent discrimination and ensure equal access for students who are pregnant or experiencing related conditions, including providing reasonable modifications, leave, and access to lactation space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.40(b)(3) provides a floor beneath which a recipient's treatment of pregnancy and pregnancy-related conditions may not fall; §106.40(b)(4) comparability applies only when consistent with those obligations. Examples: if a student requires breaks during class for pregnancy-related needs, the recipient must provide reasonable modifications consistent with §106.40(b)(3)(ii). The final regulations sometimes provide simpler processes for pregnancy because pregnancy is time-limited and needs are often foreseeable (e.g., permitting voluntary leave without additional steps that might be required for other temporary medical conditions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with disability law: pregnancy not presumed a disability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department reiterates that pregnancy standing alone is not a disability. While some pregnancy-related conditions or complications may qualify as disabilities under Section 504 or the ADA, pregnancy itself is not a disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a pregnancy-related condition qualifies as a disability, the ADA or Section 504 may apply and a recipient must comply with those obligations as well. There is no inherent conflict between these Title IX regulations and disability laws: where a recipient's disability policy is more generous, that policy must be provided; where it would be less generous than Title IX's reasonable-modification requirements, the recipient must provide the more generous benefit required under §106.40(b)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on requiring pre-participation certification for pregnant students (§106.40(b)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.40(b)(5) states that a recipient may not require a certification from a healthcare provider or any other person that a student who is pregnant or experiencing pregnancy-related conditions is physically able to participate in the recipient's class, program, or extracurricular activity, unless the certification satisfies the narrow conditions set out in §106.40(b)(5)(i)-(iii). The prohibition was expanded to include certifications by non-healthcare providers and “any other person.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provision limits burdensome and stereotype-driven documentation requests. A request for certification from someone other than a healthcare provider—such as a parent, coach, administrator, or advisor—would also be presumptively impermissible unless it meets the three statutory conditions. The rule does not prevent case-by-case safety-based participation decisions; it only prohibits discriminatory or unilateral certification requirements targeted at pregnant students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification allowed only in three narrow circumstances (§106.40(b)(5)(i)-(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient may require certification from a student (or others) only when: (i) the certified level of physical ability or health is necessary for participation in the class, program, or extracurricular activity; (ii) the recipient requires such certification of all students participating in the class, program, or extracurricular activity; and (iii) the information obtained is not used as a basis for discrimination prohibited by the Title IX regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph (b)(5)(i) pertains to the level of physical ability necessary for participation (e.g., walking at a fast pace for 20 minutes or lifting more than 50 pounds); (b)(5)(ii) means all students in the activity are asked for the same certification (not only pregnant students). Together these criteria balance recipient safety concerns with protections against discriminatory paperwork and exclusion. The information obtained must not be used to discriminate against the student.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban on certifications of emotional ability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department removed the prior regulatory reference to a student's emotional ability to participate and states recipients should never assume a student who is pregnant or experiencing pregnancy-related conditions is any less emotionally able to participate than any other student.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a recipient requires a certification of emotional ability from a pregnant student, that requirement is subject to the general prohibition on sex discrimination under §106.31(a)(1), the prohibition on pregnancy-based discrimination under §106.40(b)(1), and the requirement to provide reasonable modifications under §106.40(b)(3)(ii). If the emotional condition qualifies as a disability, ADA or Section 504 may also apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparator for determining discriminatory treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: For many purposes under these provisions, the appropriate comparator for a pregnant student is the general student population (i.e., non-pregnant students), rather than only students with non-pregnancy-related medical conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department disagrees that Young v. United Parcel Service restricts comparators here; the general student population is often the most straightforward comparator because most pregnant students will have no limitation relevant to participation. Using that comparator lets students readily identify whether they are being asked different information or subjected to different requirements and enables prompt enforcement of their rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different processes permitted when required by §106.40(b)(3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient's processes for pregnancy or related conditions may differ from those for other temporary medical conditions if treating them identically would not be consistent with §106.40(b)(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Title IX has long required that voluntary leave for pregnancy or related conditions be granted consistent with medical necessity; final §106.40(b)(3)(iv) requires that recipients permit voluntary leave for pregnancy or related conditions without requiring additional steps that might be necessary for non-pregnancy-related temporary medical conditions. The Department explains pregnancy is time-limited and needs are often foreseeable, permitting a simpler process where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of “medical or hospital” modifier in §106.40(b)(4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declined to remove the words “medical or hospital” modifying “benefit, service, plan, or policy” in §106.40(b)(4), finding the phrase not unclear in scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although commenters suggested removing the modifier to broaden protections, the Department kept the historic phrasing but indicates that the reasonable modifications framework in §106.40(b)(3) alleviates potential ambiguity about the types of supports recipients must provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.57(a) protections: parental, family, or marital status (employment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.57(a) prohibits sex discrimination against employees based on parental, family, or marital status and requires recipients to implement (revised from “apply”) nondiscriminatory treatment; the Department also revised phrasing (e.g., replacing “shall” with “must” and small wording clarifications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While commenters asked for broader protections (including reasonable modifications for parenting employees), the Department declines to require reasonable modifications for parenting employees at this time. The prohibition on different treatment based on sex stereotypes remains and has been part of the Title IX regulations for decades.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.57(b) and §106.57(c): employee pregnancy protections and comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.57(b) prohibits discrimination against employees based on current, potential, or past pregnancy or related conditions. Final §106.57(c) requires a recipient to treat an employee's pregnancy or related conditions as it does any other temporary medical condition for all job-related purposes, including commencement, duration and extensions of leave, payment of disability income, accrual of seniority and any other benefit or service, reinstatement, and under any fringe benefit offered to employees by virtue of employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department recognizes commenters' requests for reasonable modifications for employees but declines to mandate them now due to recent and pending federal legislative and regulatory action (e.g., PUMP Act, PWFA, and other rulemakings) and because §106.57(c) is broad enough to effectuate Title IX's nondiscrimination mandate for employees in its current form. The Department also notes that employees who are also students may raise overlapping issues (e.g., a student-employee needing the same stool at work and in class), but did not adopt a universal requirement to match student modifications for employees at this time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent contractor coverage optional
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declined to require that independent contractors be covered by §106.57, noting recipients are best positioned to determine who is an “employee.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may choose to cover independent contractors under §106.57 if they believe doing so will further compliance, but the Department did not mandate coverage due to the need for more information about costs, administrative burdens, interplay with common law principles, and other legal requirements. If a contractor is an employee of the recipient, that person is entitled to the protections of §106.57.
